title: With the dying
hookLine: families read Sukhmani and Japji and pray beside the dying
tomorrow: Baba Kartar is gone. what does a Sikh goodbye sound like?

cards: Hospitals at night have their own sound: a machine counting, shoes in the hall, a television murmuring behind a curtain. In Baba Kartar's room there's another sound. The family is reading in shifts.
Bebe goes first, glasses at the end of her nose, the gutka close to her face. Then Harjit. Then Simran, from the same soft-cornered book, at the place where it falls open.
After school Maya comes. She doesn't know the words, so she sits on the windowsill and holds Bebe's hand, and nobody asks her to do anything else.

teach.h: WHAT DO YOU DO AT A BEDSIDE?
teach.b: So, the question: what do you do for someone who is dying?

teach.h: STAY. LET THE WORD FILL THE ROOM.
teach.b: The Sikh answer is to stay, and to let the Guru's word fill the room. Families read Sukhmani or Japji beside the bed, and pray.
One line in Sukhmani holds the hope, Ang 278, in paraphrase: as water blends into water, so the light merges into the Light.
Then, through the curtain, Simran hears another family reading. It's Psalm 23, a song Jews and Christians both pray, in the King James words: I will fear no evil: for thou art with me.
Here's the shared thing, worth telling a friend tonight: down one hallway, two families read old words aloud so that someone dying isn't alone. Thou art with me. Sit with them.
And here's the honest difference. The psalm ends, in its own words, with dwelling in the house of the LORD for ever, a home to live in.
The Sukhmani line pictures something else: water into water, light into Light.
Two hopes, each in its own words, neither a copy of the other. Simran keeps reading. Maya keeps holding on.

how: When a Sikh is near death, family and friends sit with them and read or play Gurbani, often Sukhmani Sahib or Japji Sahib, and offer Ardas; the Sikh code of conduct asks that Gurbani be recited at the bedside.

o: saying the last rites only a priest may give
keeping children away from a sickroom
staying beside someone dying, with the Guru's word

games.q: one hallway, two rooms — tap the pairs.
p: water into water, light into Light
the house of the LORD for ever

s: at a Sikh deathbed, the family keeps quiet so as not to disturb
the Guru's word is read aloud beside the bed: Sukhmani, Japji, Ardas.
Psalm 23 is prayed by both Jews and Christians
it's in the Hebrew Bible, and Christians pray it too: thou art with me.
Sikh and Christian prayers at a deathbed picture the same afterlife
shared comfort, different pictures: a house for ever; light merging into Light.

games.q: your friend's grandfather is dying and the family is reading in Punjabi. you don't know the words. what do you do?
o: stay away; you'd only be in the way of the reading.
sit quietly with them; being there is the gift.
learn a line fast so you can join in properly.
games.why: Maya didn't know the words, so she held Bebe's hand. sit with them; the words can come from the Guru.

practice: If someone is near you, sit beside them for the sit without needing to talk. If you're alone, close your eyes and hold one person in mind, someone ill, or old, or far away, and keep them company in your thoughts.
Nothing to fix, nothing to say.

wordCard.voice: With the dying. Sikh families stay beside the bed and read Sukhmani or Japji aloud, so the room is full of the Guru's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace; Guru Arjan's long hymn, read beside the dying.

carryVoice: Keep this close: sit with them; the words can come from the Guru, or just from your hand in theirs. Go gently.
